planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall onto thin, well-drained, low-fertility soil; this small self-reseeding annual clover establishes where richer soil would favor more vigorous competitors.

directions: Knotted clover is a low, hairy winter annual legume adapted to thin, drought-prone, infertile soils where it fixes modest nitrogen and forms a short living mulch that limits erosion on rock outcrops, banks, and poor sandy ground. Broadcast seed in fall at a light rate onto a lightly scuffed seedbed, since the small seed needs good soil contact but cannot push up through heavy residue. It flowers in late spring and sets seed quickly, so for green-manure use mow or till it in at early flowering before the pinkish, unstalked flower heads dry down and scatter seed. Left undisturbed, it reseeds itself reliably on marginal sites year after year.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on heavier, moisture-retentive soils than most annual clovers tolerate; squarrose clover grows taller and more vigorously than crimson clover.

directions: Squarrose clover is an erect Mediterranean winter annual legume that produces more biomass and fodder than most other annual clovers, making it a useful nitrogen-fixing forage and green-manure crop on medium to heavy, acid-tolerant soils. Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a firm fall seedbed; the long taproot helps the stand scavenge moisture and build structure in compacted ground. Cut for hay or graze lightly in spring, then terminate by mowing or incorporation at early bloom, before the bristly, squarrose-bracted flower heads mature and shatter seed. It tolerates more acidity than crimson or Egyptian clover, broadening the soils where a self-reseeding winter legume can be grown.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in early fall onto a wide range of soil types in low-rainfall regions; gland clover carries a high proportion of hard seed, protecting the stand against false breaks.

directions: Gland clover is a densely branched, self-regenerating Mediterranean winter annual legume named for the tiny glands lining its leaflet margins; it adapts to a wider range of soils than subterranean clover and tolerates low rainfall and moderate waterlogging. Broadcast inoculated seed onto a well-prepared fall seedbed; a large fraction of the seed develops a hard coat that stays dormant through summer and softens gradually, so stands regenerate from the seed bank across multiple seasons without resowing. It fixes nitrogen while growing through winter and spring, then is grazed, cut, or left to set seed and die back naturally as soil warms. Its natural resistance to red-legged earth mite and blue-green aphid reduces establishment losses compared with many other annual clovers.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall as an alternative to annual medics in medium- to low-rainfall rotations; seed sits in non-shattering heads that can be combine-harvested with ordinary cereal equipment.

directions: Bladder clover is a semi-erect, self-regenerating Mediterranean winter annual legume whose inflated, bladder-like seed pods sit at the top of the canopy and resist shattering, a trait that makes mechanical seed harvest and natural reseeding unusually reliable. Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a firm fall seedbed as part of a ley-farming rotation on medium- to low-rainfall cropping soils. Its high level of hard seed allows it to persist through a cropping year and re-establish in the following pasture phase without resowing. For green-manure use, graze lightly or mow at flowering and incorporate before pods fully dry, leaving enough intact seed in the thatch to regenerate the stand the following season.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on salt-affected or marginal soils where more common clovers struggle; retains strong nodulation and nitrogen fixation even under salinity stress.

directions: Moroccan clover is a salt-tolerant Mediterranean annual legume used to fix nitrogen on salt-affected soils that limit more conventional forage clovers. Broadcast inoculated seed onto a fall seedbed; the species continues nodulating and fixing nitrogen even as soil salinity rises, though growth slows at the highest salt concentrations. It builds soil organic matter through winter and spring growth and is typically mowed or grazed down before summer heat, then left to self-seed where a permanent, salt-tolerant cover is wanted on reclaimed or naturally saline ground.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall at roughly 20-25 lb/acre on alkaline clay or loam soils; seedlings are vigorous and upright but intolerant of early heavy grazing, so protect young stands.

directions: Gama medic is an upright, large-seeded Mediterranean annual medic suited to truly alkaline clay and loam soils, where it fixes nitrogen and contributes substantial organic matter from its vigorous winter and spring growth. Broadcast seed in fall and avoid grazing or mowing too early, since seedlings are easily grazed out before they establish a deep enough root system. For a persistent, self-reseeding stand, lightly incorporate the large, spine-covered seed pods into the surface every other year by disking or harrowing in late summer, which helps bury seed and maintain the population on alkaline ground where few other annual legumes compete well.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-inoculated seed with a strain-specific Rhizobium, since this species nodulates poorly with generic medic inoculants in soils where it has not previously grown.

directions: Tifton burclover is a self-supporting annual medic from the dry cropping regions of West Asia, grown as a nitrogen-fixing legume in ley-farming rotations similar to barrel and burclover. Because it is highly strain-specific for effective nodulation, sow seed inoculated with a Rhizobium strain known to work with this species rather than a generic medic blend. Broadcast into a fall seedbed on calcareous or neutral soils; the stand builds organic matter and fixes nitrogen through winter and spring, then is grazed, mowed, or incorporated in late spring before seed pods fully dry, leaving some seed to regenerate the stand the following autumn.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-inoculated seed alongside a cereal companion for climbing support; tolerates light, medium, and heavy soils across a range of pH.

directions: Bard vetch is a climbing Mediterranean annual legume, long used as livestock feed and, in parts of the Mediterranean, as a grain for human food, that fixes nitrogen on a wide range of soil textures. Sow inoculated seed in fall mixed with a cereal grain such as oats or rye, which gives the climbing vines structure to scramble up as they grow. The stand builds organic matter and nitrogen through winter and early spring; terminate by mowing or crimping at early-to-mid bloom before pods fill, timing similar to common vetch, so stems have time to break down before the next planting.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-inoculated seed into average, well-drained soil with a cereal companion for support; a drought-resistant relic forage legume once grown in Iberia and southern France.

directions: Oneflower vetch is a scrambling Mediterranean annual legume, once cultivated for forage, green manure, and its edible seed on the Iberian Peninsula and in southern France, though it survives today mainly as a relic crop. It fixes nitrogen via root nodules and tolerates drought well once established, making it a candidate for low-input, dry-farmed cover cropping. Direct sow in fall with a cereal or grass companion for the clinging stems to climb; mow or incorporate at bloom to release nitrogen before pods mature, following a termination timing similar to other Mediterranean annual vetches.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-inoculated seed with a cereal companion; accumulates unusually high crude protein in its foliage among Mediterranean annual vetches.

directions: Wandering vetch is a slender, climbing Mediterranean annual legume valued historically as fodder for its high crude-protein green mass, and a nitrogen fixer through its root nodules. Direct sow inoculated seed in fall alongside a supportive cereal companion, since the thin, branched stems climb rather than stand upright. Growth continues through the cool season, and the stand should be mowed or incorporated at flowering before seed set, both to maximize nitrogen release into the soil and to prevent volunteer seedlings, following the same general termination window used for other annual vetches.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-inoculated seed with a cereal or grass companion for the winged, climbing stems to lean on.

directions: Annual pea is a Mediterranean winged-stemmed legume grown regionally as fodder, fixing nitrogen through root nodules while producing substantial green biomass for a winter annual. Direct sow inoculated seed in fall with a cereal companion to support its tall, scrambling growth. Allow it to grow through the cool season, then mow or incorporate at flowering before seed pods fill, a termination window comparable to chickling vetch and other annual Lathyrus cover crops, to add organic matter and release fixed nitrogen ahead of the next planting.

planting.note: Sow after the last frost once soil is warm; grown widely in East African maize-bean rotations as a fast-biomass green manure legume.

directions: Slenderleaf crotalaria is a tall, fast-growing tropical legume used in Africa as a green manure in rotation with maize and beans, where incorporating it ahead of the next legume crop has been shown to lift subsequent bean yields well above a continuous cereal-legume rotation. Broadcast or drill seed into warm soil after frost danger passes; the plant reaches up to about 8 feet within 3-5 months, fixing nitrogen and producing a heavy flush of biomass. Terminate by cutting and incorporating at flowering, before stems become fibrous and woody, to maximize the nitrogen and organic matter returned to the soil ahead of the following crop.

planting.note: Sow after last frost on warm soil; like sunn hemp, this Crotalaria fixes nitrogen rapidly but can self-seed aggressively, so monitor and remove volunteers outside the intended planting area.

directions: Lanceleaf crotalaria is a woody-based tropical legume grown as a green manure for its rapid nitrogen fixation and heavy foliage production, which adds organic matter and improves soil structure when incorporated. Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; growth is vigorous through the warm season but is killed back by any hard frost. Terminate by mowing or tilling in at flowering, before stems lignify, since mature growth decomposes slowly; because this species has escaped cultivation and naturalized as a weed in some regions, remove any volunteer seedlings that appear outside the planting area in subsequent seasons.

planting.note: Sow shallowly in fall on sandy, acidic, low-phosphorus soils where most clovers fail; inoculate with an Ornithopus-specific rhizobium before first planting a field.

directions: Slender serradella is a fine-leaved annual legume that, like the closely related French serradella, thrives on sandy, acidic, infertile soils where it fixes nitrogen with far less phosphorus than clovers or medics require. Sow rhizobium-inoculated seed shallowly in fall on well-drained, low-fertility ground; establishment is gradual but the stand builds biomass through winter and spring without the need for heavy fertility inputs. Mow or graze lightly before incorporating to add organic matter ahead of a following crop, or allow it to self-seed as a low-maintenance legume ground cover in orchards and vineyards on acid, sandy soils.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on low-lying, saline, winter-waterlogged ground where common clovers and medics fail; inoculate seed with a salt-tolerant rhizobial strain for best nodulation.

directions: Messina is a salt- and waterlogging-tolerant annual legume, bred from Mediterranean wild Melilotus siculus populations for saltland pastures, that fixes nitrogen and builds organic matter on soils too saline or seasonally wet for conventional clovers and medics. Broadcast inoculated seed onto saline or low, winter-wet ground in fall; the aerial-seeding habit lets it produce and shed seed above the waterline even when the root zone is periodically flooded. It grows through winter and spring, and the stand can be grazed, mown, or left to die back and reseed naturally as salinity and waterlogging allow, requiring no tillage to persist in reclaimed saline paddocks.
